# Fast approximation of search trees on trees with centroid trees **Abstract** Search trees on trees (STTs) generalize the fundamental binary search tree (BST) data structure: in STTs the underlying search space is an arbitrary tree, whereas in BSTs it is _a path_. An optimal BST of size _n_ can be computed for a given distribution of queries in O(_n_2) time [Knuth, Acta Inf. 1971] and _centroid_ BSTs provide a nearly-optimal alternative, computable in O(_n_) time [Mehlhorn, SICOMP 1977]. By contrast, optimal STTs are not known to be computable in polynomial time, and the fastest constant-approximation algorithm runs in O(_n_3) time [Berendsohn, Kozma, SODA 2022]. Centroid trees can be defined for STTs analogously to BSTs, and they have been used in a wide range of algorithmic applications. In the unweighted case (i.e., for a uniform distribution of queries), the centroid tree can be computed in O(_n_) time [Brodal, Fagerberg, Pedersen, Östlin, ICALP 2001; Della Giustina, Prezza, Venturini, SPIRE 2019]. These algorithms, however, do not readily extend to the weighted case. Moreover, no approximation guarantees were previously known for centroid trees in either the unweighted or weighted cases. In this paper we revisit centroid trees in a general, weighted setting, and we settle both the algorithmic complexity of constructing them, and the quality of their approximation. For constructing a weighted centroid tree, we give an _output-sensitive_ \(\mathcal{O}(nlogn)\subseteq\mathcal{O}(nlogn)\) time algorithm, where _h_ is the height of the resulting centroid tree. If the weights are of polynomial complexity, the running time is O(_n_loglog_n_). We show these bounds to be optimal, in a general decision tree model of computation. For approximation, we prove that the cost of a centroid tree is at most _twice_ the optimum, and this guarantee is best possible, both in the weighted and unweighted cases. We also give tight, fine-grained bounds on the approximation-ratio for bounded-degree trees and on the approximation-ratio of more general \(\alpha\)-centroid trees. ### 1 Introduction Search trees on trees (STTs) are a far-reaching generalization of binary search trees (BSTs), modeling the exploration of tree-shaped search spaces. Given an undirected tree T , an STT on T is a tree rooted at an arbitrary vertex _r_ of T , with subtrees built recursively on the components resulting after removing _r_ from T , see Figure 1 for an example. BSTs correspond to the special case where the underlying tree T is a _path_. STTs and, more generally, search trees on graphs arise in several different contexts and have been studied under different names: _tubings_ [CD06], _vertex rankings_ [DKKM94, BDJ+98, ES14], _ordered color- ings_ [KMS95], _elimination trees_ [Liu90, PSL90, AH94, BGHK95]. STTs have been crucial in many algorithmic applications, e.g., in pattern matching and counting [Fer13, KPR+14, GHLW15], cache-oblivious data struc- tures [BFCK06, FV16], tree clustering [FJ83], geometric visibility [GHL+87], planar point location [GT98], distance oracles [CGMW21]. <tbc>Similarly to the setting of BSTs, a natural goal is to find an STT in which the expected depth of a vertex is as small as possible; we refer to such a tree as an _optimal tree_, noting that it is not necessarily unique. This optimization task can be studied both for the uniform probability distribution over the vertices, and for the more general case of an arbitrary distribution given as input. We refer to the first as the _unweighted_ and the second as the _weighted_ problem.

For BSTs, both the unweighted and the weighted problems are well-understood. In the unweighted case, a simple balanced binary tree achieves the optimum. In the weighted case, an optimal tree on _n_ vertices can be found in time O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) by Knuth’s algorithm \[Knu71\], a textbook example of dynamic programming. No faster algorithm is known in general, although Larmore’s algorithm \[Lar87\] achieves better bounds under certain regularity assumptions on the weights; for example, if the probability assigned to each vertex is \(\Omega(1/n)\), then the optimum can be found in time O(_n_<sup>1.591</sup>).

By contrast, the complexity of computing an optimal STT is far less understood. Even in the unweighted case, no polynomial-time algorithm is known, and the problem is not known to be NP-hard even with arbitrary weights. Recently, a PTAS was given for the weighted problem \[BK22\], but its running time for obtaining a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation of the optimal STT is \(\mathcal{O}(n^{1+2/\varepsilon})\), which is prohibitive for reasonably small values of \(\varepsilon\). Note that the apparently easier problem of minimizing the _maximum depth_ of a vertex, i.e., computing the _treedepth_ of a tree, can be solved in linear time by Schäffer’s algorithm \[Sch89\], and treedepth itself has many algorithmic applications, e.g., see \[NdM12, §6,7\].

## Centroid trees.

Given the relatively high cost of computing optimal binary search trees, research has turned already half a century ago to efficient approximations. Mehlhorn has shown \[Meh75, Meh77\] that a simple BST that can be computed in O(_n_) time closely approximates the optimum. More precisely, both the optimum cost and the cost of the obtained tree are in \[_H/_log(3)_,H_+1\], where _H_ is the binary entropy of the input distribution.<sup>1</sup> Alternatively, the cost can be upper bounded by `OPT`+log(`OPT`)+log_e_, where `OPT` is the cost of the optimal tree. Observe that this means that the approximation ratio gets arbitrarily close to 1 as `OPT` goes to infinity. <sup>2</sup>

The BST that achieves the above guarantees is built by recursively picking roots such as to make the weights of the left and right subtrees "as equal as possible". This is a special case of a _centroid tree_, defined as follows. Given a tree T , a _centroid_ of T is a vertex whose removal from T results in components with<tbc>

Extending such a model to STTs is straightforward, but perhaps less natural in the case of general trees, we therefore omit it for the sake of simplicity, and consider only successful searches.

The fact that an (unweighted) centroid always exists was already shown in the 19-th century by C. Jordan \[Jor69\]. We sketch the easy, constructive argument that also shows the existence of a weighted centroid: start at an arbitrary vertex of T and, as long as the current vertex is not a centroid, move one edge in the direction of the component with largest weight. It is not hard to see that the procedure succeeds, visiting each vertex at most once.

A straightforward implementation of the above procedure finds an unweighted centroid tree in O(_n_log_n_) time. This running time has been improved to O(_n_) by carefully using data structures \[BFPÖ01, GPV19\]. The run-time guarantees however, do not readily generalize from the unweighted to the weighted setting. Intuitively, the difficulty lies in the fact that in the weighted case, the removal of a centroid vertex may split the tree in a very unbalanced way, leaving up to _n_-1 vertices in one component. Thus, a naive recursive approach will take \(\Theta(n^2)\) time in the worst case.

Most algorithmic applications of STTs, including those mentioned before, rely on centroid trees. It is therefore surprising that nothing appears to be known about how well the centroid tree approximates the optimal STT in either the unweighted or weighted cases. In this paper we prove that the centroid tree is a 2-approximation of the optimal STT, and that the factor 2 is, in general, best possible, both in the unweighted and weighted settings. As our main result, we also show a more precise bound on the approximation ratio of centroid trees, in terms of the maximum degree of the underlying tree T .<sup>3</sup>

Before stating our results, we need a few definitions. Consider an undirected, unrooted tree T given as input, together with a _weight function_ \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). For convenience, for any subgraph H of T , we denote \(w(\mathcal{H})=\sum_{x\in V(\mathcal{H})}w(x)\). (To interpret the weights as probabilities, we need the condition _w_(T)=1. It is, however, often convenient to relax this requirement and allow arbitrary non-negative weights, which is the approach we take in this paper.)

A _search tree_ on T is a rooted tree _T_ with vertex set _V_(T) whose root is an arbitrary vertex \(r\in V(\mathcal{T})\). The children of _r_ in _T_ are the roots of search trees built on the connected components of the forest T-_r_. A tree consisting of a single vertex admits only itself as a search tree. (See Figure 1.) It follows from the definition that for all _x_, the subtree _T<sub>x</sub>_ of _T_ rooted at _x_ induces a connected subgraph T\[_V(T<sub>x</sub>_)\] of T , and moreover, _T<sub>x</sub>_ is a search tree on T\[_V(T<sub>x</sub>_)\].

The _cost_ of a search tree _T_ on T is \(\mathtt{cost}_w(T)=\sum_{x\in V(T)}w(x)\cdot\mathtt{depth}_T(x)\), where the depth of the root is taken to be 1. The _optimum cost_ `OPT`(T_,w_) is the minimum of `cost`_<sub>w</sub>(T_) over all search trees _T_ of T .

A vertex \(v\in V(\mathcal{T})\) is a _centroid_ if for all components H of T-_v_, we have \(w(\mathcal{H})\le w(\mathcal{T})/2\). A search tree _T_ of T is a _centroid tree_ if vertex _x_ is a centroid of T\[_V(T<sub>x</sub>_)\] for all \(x\in V(\mathcal{T})\). In general, the centroid tree is not unique, and centroid trees of the same tree can have different costs.<sup>4</sup> We denote by `cent`(T_,w_) the _maximum_ cost of a centroid tree of (T_,w_), with weight function _w_.

We can now state our approximation guarantee for centroid trees.

**Theorem 1.1.** _Let_ T _be a tree,_ \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\)_, and m=w_(T)_. Then_

\(\mathtt{cent}(\mathcal{T},w)\le 2\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T},w)-m.\)

We show that this result is optimal, including in the additive term. Moreover, the constant factor 2 cannot be improved even for unweighted instances.

**Theorem 1.2.**<tbc>

_(i) For every_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _there is a sequence of instances_ (T_<sub>n</sub>,w<sub>n</sub>_) _with w<sub>n</sub>_(T_<sub>n</sub>_)=1_, and for every centroid tree C<sub>n</sub> of_ (T_<sub>n</sub>,w<sub>n</sub>_)<tbc>

\(\mathtt{cost}_{w_n}(C_n)\ge 2\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)-1-\varepsilon.\)

<sup>3</sup>In their recent paper on dynamic STTs, Bose, Cardinal, Iacono, Koumoutsos, and Langerman \[BCI<sup>+</sup>20\] remark that the ratio between the costs of the centroid- and optimal trees may be unbounded. In light of our results, this observation is erroneous. It is true, however, that a centroid tree built using the uniform distribution may be far from the optimum w.r.t. a different distribution. <sup>4</sup>Consider, for instance the two different centroid trees of a path on four vertices, with weights (0.2,0.3,0.2,0.3).

(_ii)_ _There is a sequence of instances_ (T_<sub>n</sub>,w<sub>n</sub>), where w<sub>n</sub> is the uniform distribution on V_(T_<sub>n</sub>), and for every centroid tree C<sub>n</sub> of_ (T_<sub>n</sub>,w<sub>n</sub>_)<tbc>

<tbc>\(lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathtt{cost}_{w_n}(C_n)}{\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)}=2.\)<tbc>

<tbc>_In both cases_ \(lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)=\infty\).

Note that the fact that \(lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)=\infty\) in Theorem 1.2 establishes that the _asymptotic_ approximation ratio is 2. By this we mean that every bound of the form \(\mathtt{cent}\le c\cdot\mathtt{OPT}+o(\mathtt{OPT})\) must have \(c\ge 2\).

We next show a stronger guarantee when the underlying tree has bounded degree.

**Theorem 1.3.** _Let_ T _be a tree,_ \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\)_, and let_ \(\Delta\) _be the_ maximum degree _of_ T_. Then_

\(\mathtt{cent}(\mathcal{T},w)\le\left(2-\frac{1}{2^\Delta}\right)\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T},w).\)

We complement this result by two lower bounds. The first establishes the tightness of the approximation ratio. The second shows a (slightly smaller) lower bound on the approximation ratio for instances where `OPT` is unbounded.

**Theorem 1.4.** _Let_ \(\Delta\ge 3\) _be integer._

(_i)_ _There is a sequence of instances_ (T_<sub>n</sub>,w<sub>n</sub>_) _such that_ T_<sub>n</sub> has maximum degree at most_ \(\Delta\)_, and for every centroid tree C<sub>n</sub> of_ (T_<sub>n</sub>,w<sub>n</sub>_)<tbc>

<tbc>\(lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathtt{cost}_{w_n}(C_n)}{\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)}=2-\frac{1}{2^\Delta}.\)<tbc>

_(ii)_ _There is a sequence of instances_ (T_<sub>n</sub>,w<sub>n</sub>_) _such that_ T_<sub>n</sub> has maximum degree at most_ \(\Delta\), \(lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)=\infty\)_, w<sub>n</sub>_(T_<sub>n</sub>_)=1_, and for every centroid tree C<sub>n</sub> of_ (T_<sub>n</sub>,w<sub>n</sub>_)

<tbc>\(\mathtt{cost}_{w_n}(C_n)\ge\left(2-\frac{4}{2^\Delta}\right)\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)-1.\)

We remark that Theorem 1.4(i) does not exclude the possibility of a bound of the form \(\mathtt{cent}\le c\cdot\mathtt{OPT}+o(\mathtt{OPT})\), where \(c<2-\frac{1}{2^\Delta}\), as here `OPT`(T_<sub>n</sub>,w<sub>n</sub>_) is bounded. Part (ii), however, establishes that a bound of the form \(\mathtt{cent}\le c\cdot\mathtt{OPT}+o(\mathtt{OPT})\) must have \(c\ge 2-\frac{4}{2^\Delta}\). We leave open the problem of closing the gap in the asymptotic approximation ratio in terms of \(\Delta\).

## Computing centroid trees.

On the algorithmic side, we show that the weighted centroid tree can be computed in O(_n_log_n_) time. Previously, the fastest known constant-approximation algorithm \[BK22\] took O(_n_<sup>3</sup>) time (similarly achieving an approximation ratio of 2). The main step of our algorithm, finding the weighted centroid of a tree, is achievable in O(log_n_) time, assuming that the underlying tree is stored in a _top tree_ data structure \[AHLT05\]. Iterating this procedure in combination with known algorithms for _constructing_ and _splitting_ top trees yields the algorithm that runs in O(_n_log_n_) time. We also develop an improved, _output-sensitive_ algorithm, with running time O(_n_log_h_), where _h_ is the height of the resulting centroid tree, yielding a running time O(_n_loglog_n_) in the typical case when the height is O(log_n_).

**Theorem 1.5.** _Let_ T _be a tree on n vertices and w be a weight function. We can compute a centroid tree of_ (T_,w_) _in time_ O(_n_log_h), where h is the height of the computed centroid tree._

One may ask whether the weighted centroid tree can be computed in linear time, similarly to the unweighted centroid tree, or to the weighted centroid BST. We show that, assuming a general decision tree model of computation, this is not possible, and the algorithm of Theorem 1.5 is optimal for all _n_ and _h_ (up to<tbc>

a constant factor). Our lower bound on the running time applies, informally, to any deterministic algorithm in which the input weights affect program flow only in the form of binary decisions, involving arbitrary computable functions. The model thus excludes using the weights for addressing memory, e.g., via hashing. More precisely, consider a tree T on _n_ vertices. We say that a _binary decision tree D_T _solves_ T for a class of weight functions W mapping _V_(T) to \(\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), if the leaves of _D_T are search trees on T , every branching of _D_T is of the form "\(f(w)\ge 0\)?" for some computable function \(f:\mathcal{W}\rightarrow\{-1,+1\}\), and for every weight function \(w\in\mathcal{W}\), starting from the root of _D_T and following branchings down the tree, we reach a leaf _T_ of _D_T that is a valid centroid tree for (T_,w_). The height of _D_T is then a lower bound on the worst-case running time. **Theorem 1.6.** _Let_ \(h\ge 3\) _and_ \(n\ge h+1\) _be integers. Then there is a tree_ T _on at most n vertices and a class_ W _of weight functions on V_(T) _such that for every_ \(w\in\mathcal{W}\)_, every centroid tree of_ (T_,w_) _has height h, and every binary decision tree that solves_ T _for_ W _has height_ \(\Omega(nlogh)\). We can nonetheless improve the running time, when the weights are restricted in certain (natural) ways. We define the _spread_ \(\sigma\) of a weight function _w_ as the ratio between the total weight _w_(T), and the smallest _non-zero_ weight of a vertex. As we show, \(\mathcal{O}(nlogh)\subseteq\mathcal{O}(nloglog\left(\sigma+n\right))\) and therefore, when \(\sigma\in n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\) (for instance, if the weights are integers stored in RAM words), we obtain a running time of O(_n_loglog_n_). When many vertices have zero weight, we obtain further improvements, e.g., if only O(_n/_log_n_) of the weights are non-zero, we can compute a centroid tree in O(_n_) time, even if the height _h_ is large. We defer the precise statement of these refined bounds and the discussion of their optimality to Section 5. ## Approximate centroid trees. Finally, we consider the approximation guarantees of a generalized form of centroid trees. Let us call a vertex _v_ of a tree T an \(\alpha\)-centroid, for \(0\le\alpha\le 1\), if \(w(\mathcal{H})\le\alpha\cdot w(\mathcal{T})\), for all components H of T-_v_. An \(\alpha\)-centroid tree is an STT in which every vertex _x_ is an \(\alpha\)-centroid of its subtree T\[_V(Tx_)\]. Observe that the standard centroid tree is a \(\frac{1}{2}\)-centroid tree, and all STTs are 1-centroid trees. Also note that an \(\alpha\)-centroid is a \(\beta\)-centroid for all \(\beta\ge\alpha\) and that the existence of an \(\alpha\)-centroid is not guaranteed for \(\alpha<\frac{1}{2}\) (consider a single edge with the two endpoints having the same weight). On the other hand, an \(\alpha\)-centroid for \(\alpha<\frac{1}{2}\), if it exists, is unique, and therefore the \(\alpha\)-centroid tree is also unique. To see this, consider an \(\alpha\)-centroid _c_ that splits T into components T1_,...,_T_k_. If an alternative \(\alpha\)-centroid \(c'\) were in component T_i_, then its removal would yield a component containing all vertices in T-_V_(T_i_), of weight at least \((1-\alpha)\cdot w(\mathcal{T})>\alpha\cdot w(\mathcal{T})\). Denote by \(\mathtt{cent}^\alpha(\mathcal{T},w)\) the maximum cost of an \(\alpha\)-centroid tree of (T_,w_), or 0 if no \(\alpha\)-centroid tree exists. We refine our guarantee from Theorem 1.1 to approximate centroid trees: **Theorem 1.7.** _Let_ T _be a tree,_ \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\)_, m=w_(T)_. We have_ \((i)\mathtt{cent}^\alpha(\mathcal{T},w)\le\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T},w)-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}m,\text{\textit{for}}\alpha\in(0,1),\)
\((ii)\mathtt{cent}^\alpha(\mathcal{T},w)\le\frac{1}{2-3\alpha}\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T},w)-\frac{3\alpha-1}{2-3\alpha}m,\text{\textit{for}}\alpha\in\left[\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}\right].\) Note that the second bound is a strengthening of the first when \(\alpha<\frac{1}{2}\). In particular, for \(\alpha\le\frac{1}{3}\), it implies that an \(\alpha\)-centroid tree is _optimal_, if it exists. We show that the result is tight when \(\alpha\ge\frac{1}{2}\) by proving a matching lower bound. **Theorem 1.8.** _For every_ \(\alpha\in[\frac{1}{2},1)\) _there is a sequence of instances_ (T_n,wn_) _with_ \(lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)=\infty\)_, wn_(T_n_)=1 _and_ \(\mathtt{cent}^\alpha(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)\ge\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}.\) Note that if \(\alpha>\frac{1}{2}\), we cannot prove such a lower bound for _all_ \(\alpha\)-centroid trees of (T_n,wn_) (as in Theorem 1.2), since a \(\frac{1}{2}\)-centroid tree exists and has stronger approximation guarantees according to Theorem 1.1.

Finally, we argue that every optimal STT is a \(\frac{2}{3}\)-centroid tree. A special case of this result (for BSTs) was shown by Hirschberg, Larmore, and Molodowitch \[HLM86\], who also showed that the ratio \(\frac{2}{3}\) is tight (in the special case of BSTs, and thus, also for STTs).

**Theorem 1.9.** _Let T be an optimal STT of_ (T_,w). Then, T is a_ \(\frac{2}{3}\)_-centroid tree of_ (T_,w)._

### Structure of the paper.

In Section 2 we state a number of technical results needed in the proofs. In Section 3 we prove the general upper and lower bounds on the approximation ratio of centroid trees (Theorems 1.1 and 1.2). In Section 4 we prove the fine-grained bounds on the approximation ratio of centroid trees (Theorems 1.3 and 1.4). Section 5 contains the algorithmic results (Theorem 1.5 and extensions) and the lower bounds (Theorems 1.6 and extensions). Results on \(\alpha\)-centroids (Theorems 1.7, 1.8, and 1.9) are proved in Section 6. In Section 7 we conclude with open questions.

### Related work.

Different models of searching in trees have also been considered, e.g., the one where we query edges instead of vertices \[BFN99, LN01, MOW08, OP06\], with connections to searching in posets \[LS85, HIT11\]. In the edge-query setting, Cicalese, Jacobs, Laber and Molinaro \[CJLM11, CJLM14\] study the problem of minimizing the average search time of a vertex, and show this to be an NP-hard problem \[CJLM11\]. They also show that an "edge-centroid" tree (in their terminology, a greedy algorithm) gives a 1.62-approximation of the optimum \[CJLM14\].

STTs generalize BSTs, therefore it is natural to ask to what extent the theory developed for BSTs can be extended to STTs. Defining a natural _rotation_ operation on STTs, Bose, Cardinal, Iacono, Koumoutsos, and Langerman \[BCI<sup>+</sup>20\] develop an _O_(loglog_n_) competitive dynamic STT, analogously to Tango BSTs \[DHIP07\]. In a similar spirit, Berendsohn and Kozma \[BK22\] generalize Splay trees \[ST85\] to STTs. The rotation operation on STTs naturally leads to the definition of _tree associahedra_, a combinatorial structure that extends the classical associahedron defined over BSTs or other Catalan-structures. Properties of tree- and more general graph associahedra have been studied in \[CD06, Dev09, CMPP15, CLP18, CPV21, Ber22\].

Searching in trees and graphs has also been motivated with applications, including file system synchronisation \[BFN99, MOW08\], software testing \[BFN99, MOW08\], asymmetric communication protocols \[LM11\], VLSI layout \[Lei80\], and assembly planning \[IRV88\].

## 2 Preliminaries

Given a graph _G_, we denote by _V(G_) its set of vertices, by _E(G_) its set of edges, and by C(_G_) its set of connected components. If \(v\in V(G)\), denote by _N<sub>G</sub>(v_) the set of neighbors of _v_ in _G_, and deg_<sub>G</sub>(v_)=|_N<sub>G</sub>(v_)|. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), denote by _G_\[_S_\] the subgraph of _G_ induced by _S_, and for brevity, _G-v=G_\[_V(G_)-{_v_}\], and _G-S=G_\[_V(G_)-_S_\].

The following observation is straightforward.

**Observation 2.1.** _Let T be a search tree on_ T , \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\)_, m=w_(T) _and r_=`root`(_T). For each component_ \(\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-r)\)_, denote by T_<sub>H</sub> _the subtree of T rooted at the unique child of r in_ H_. Then_

\(\mathtt{cost}_w(T)=m+\sum_{\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-r)}\mathtt{cost}_w(T_\mathcal{H})\ge m+\sum_{\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-r)}\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{H},w).\)

Given a search tree _T_ on a tree T and a subgraph H of T , we denote by `LCA`_<sub>T</sub>_(H) the vertex with maximal depth in _T_ that is an ancestor of all vertices of H.

The following two technical lemmas will be useful later.

**Lemma 2.1.** _Let T be a search tree on_ T _and_ H _a connected subgraph of_ T _. Then_ \(\mathtt{LCA}_T(\mathcal{H})\in V(\mathcal{H})\).

_Proof._ Denote \(\ell=\mathtt{LCA}_T(\mathcal{H})\) and assume \(\ell\notin V(\mathcal{H})\). Denote \(\tilde{\mathcal{H}}=\mathcal{T}[V(T_\ell)]\). We have \(\mathcal{H}\subseteq\tilde{\mathcal{H}}\). Since H is connected, between every two vertices of H, there is a path in \(\tilde{\mathcal{H}}\) that does not go through \(\ell\). It follows that \(\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{C}\) for some connected component \(\mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{C}(\tilde{\mathcal{H}}-\ell)\). Then `LCA`_<sub>T</sub>_(C) is a child of \(\ell\) and an ancestor of all the vertices in H, a contradiction to the choice of \(\ell\).

**Lemma 2.2.** _Let_ T _be a tree with weight function w, and let_ A, B _be connected subgraphs of_ T _. If_ A _and_ B _each contain a centroid of_ (T_,w), and_ \(V(\mathcal{A})\cap V(\mathcal{B})\neq\emptyset\)_, then_ \(V(\mathcal{A})\cap V(\mathcal{B})\) _contains a centroid of_ (T_,w)._

_Proof._ Let \(c_1\in\mathcal{A}\) and \(c_2\in\mathcal{B}\) be centroids. If \(c_1\in V(\mathcal{A})\cap V(\mathcal{B})\) or \(c_2\in V(\mathcal{A})\cap V(\mathcal{B})\), we are done. Let \(\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-c)\). Note that either \(c_1\notin V(\mathcal{M})\) or \(c_2\notin V(\mathcal{M})\). Assume w.l.o.g., that \(c_1\notin V(\mathcal{M})\). Then \(V(\mathcal{M})\subseteq V(\mathcal{M}')\) for some component \(\mathcal{M}'\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-c_1)\), and so \(w(\mathcal{M})\le w(\mathcal{M}')\le\frac{1}{2}w(\mathcal{T})\). This concludes the proof.

## Projection of a search tree.

For a rooted tree _T_ and a vertex \(v\in V(T)\), we denote by `Path`_<sub>T</sub>(v_) the set of vertices on the path in _T_ from `root`(_T_) to _v_, including both endpoints. The proofs of our upper bounds require the following notion of _projection_ of a search tree.

**Theorem 2.1.** _Let T be a search tree on_ T _and_ H _a connected subgraph of_ T _. There is a unique search tree T_|<sub>H</sub> _on_ H _such that for every_ \(v\in V(\mathcal{H})\),

\(\mathtt{Path}_{T|_\mathcal{H}}(v)=\mathtt{Path}_T(v)\cap V(\mathcal{H}).\)

**Definition 2.1** (Projection)**.** _Let T be a search tree on_ T _and_ H _a connected subgraph of_ T _. We call T_|<sub>H</sub>_, whose existence is established by Theorem 2.1, the projection of T to_ H.

An equivalent notion of projection was used by Cardinal, Langerman and Perez-Lantero \[CLP18\] without explicitly stating Theorem 2.1, and a closely related notion was used by Cicalese, Jacobs, Laber and Molinaro \[CJLM14\] in the edge-query setting. In Appendix A we prove Theorem 2.1, present the definition of a projection used by Cardinal et al. and show that the two definitions are equivalent.

## Median and centroid.

A certain concept of a _median vertex_ of a tree has been used previously in the literature. If T is a tree with positive vertex weights and positive edge weights, then the median of T is the vertex _v_ minimizing the quantity \(\sum_{u\neq v}w(u)\cdot d(u,v)\). Here _w(u_) is the weight of the vertex _u_, and _d(u,v_) is the distance from _u_ to _v_, i.e., the sum of the edge weights on the path from _u_ to _v_. We show (proof in Appendix B) that if all edge-weights are 1, then medians are precisely centroids.

**Lemma 2.3.** _Let_ T _be a graph and w be a weight function on V_(T)_. For each_ \(u\in V(\mathcal{T})\)_, define_ \(W(u)=\sum_{v\in V(\mathcal{T})}d_\mathcal{T}(u,v)\cdot w(v)\)_, where d_<sub>T</sub>(_u,v_) _denotes the number of edges on the path from u to v in_ T _. Then_ \(c\in V(\mathcal{T})\) _is a centroid of_ (T_,w_) _if and only if W(c_) _is minimal._

## Breaking ties.

Our lower bounds require the following tie-breaking procedure, with proof in Appendix C.

**Lemma 2.4.** _Let_ T _be a tree,_ \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) _a weight function and let C be a centroid tree of_ (T_,w). For every_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _there exists a weight function_ \(w':V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) _such that C is the unique centroid tree of_ \((\mathcal{T},w')\) _and_ \(\|w'-w\|_\infty<\varepsilon\).

## Contractions in weighted trees.

Let T be a tree, let \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) be a weight function, and let {_u,v_} be an edge of T . Then _contracting_ {_u,v_} produces a tree \(\mathcal{T}'\) and a weight function \(w'\), defined as follows. The tree \(\mathcal{T}'\) is obtained from T by removing _u_ and _v_, adding a new vertex _s_, and setting \(N_{\mathcal{T}^\prime}(s)=N_\mathcal{T}(u)\cup N_\mathcal{T}(v)-\{u,v\}\). The weight function \(w'\) is defined as \(w'(s)=w(u)+w(v)\) and \(w'(x)=w(x)\) for \(x\in V(\mathcal{T}')-\{s\}\).

The lemma below shows that contractions essentially preserve centroids.

**Lemma 2.5.** _Let_ T _be a tree and_ \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) _be a weight function, and let_ \(\mathcal{T}',w'\) _be obtained from_ T_,w by contracting the edge_ {_u,v_} _into a new vertex s. Then s is a centroid of_ \((\mathcal{T}',w')\) _if and only if u or v is a centroid of_ (T_,w); and x is a centroid of_ \((\mathcal{T}',w')\) _if and only if x is a centroid of_ (T_,w), for each_ \(x\in V(\mathcal{T}')-\{s\}\).

_Proof._ W.l.o.g., assume that _w_(T)=1. Consider first a vertex \(x\in V(\mathcal{T})-\{u,v\}\). The contraction {_u,v_} does not change the weight of any component \(\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-x)\). Thus, _x_ is a centroid of (T_,w_) if and only if it is a centroid of \((\mathcal{T}',w')\). Consider now the vertices _u_, _v_, and _s_. Observe that \(\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-\{u,v\})=\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}'-s)\), and the contraction does not affect the weights of these components. If _u_ or _v_ is a centroid of (T_,w_), then no component of C(T-{_u,v_}) has weight more than \(\frac{1}{2}\). Thus, _s_ is a centroid of \((\mathcal{T}',w')\). On the other hand, suppose that _s_ is a centroid of \((\mathcal{T}',w')\). Consider a component \(\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-u)\). If H does not contain _v_, then \(\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-\{u,v\})=\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}'-s)\), so \(w(\mathcal{H})\le\frac{1}{2}\) by assumption. In the same way, for each \(\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-v)\), if H does not contain _u_, then \(w(\mathcal{H})\le\frac{1}{2}\). Now let H_v_ be the component of T-_u_ that contains _v_, and let H_u_ be the component of T-_v_ that contains _u_. Since H_v_ and H_u_ are disjoint, we have \(w(\mathcal{H}_v)+w(\mathcal{H}_u)\le 1\), so either \(w(\mathcal{H}_v)\le\frac{1}{2}\) or \(w(\mathcal{H}_u)\le\frac{1}{2}\). ## 5.1 Output-sensitive algorithm

We now improve the algorithm given above to run in time O(_n_log_h_), where _n_ is the number of vertices in T and _h_ is the height of the computed centroid tree.

The main idea of the algorithm is inspired by the linear-time algorithm for _unweighted_ centroids by Della Giustina, Prezza, and Venturini \[GPV19\]. Instead of building a top tree on the whole tree T , we first split T into connected subgraphs of size roughly _h_, and build a top tree on each component. Contracting each component into a single vertex yields _super-vertices_ in a _super-tree_. Each search for a centroid consists of a global search and a local search: We first find the super-vertex containing the centroid, then we find the centroid within that super-vertex. After finding the centroid, we remove it, which may split up the super-vertex into multiple super-vertices with a top tree each, and also may split the super-tree into a super-forest. Finally, we recurse on each component of the super-forest.

It can be seen that the total number of top tree operations needed is O(_n_). Since the top trees each contain only _h_ vertices, a top tree operation takes O(log_h_) time, for a total of O(_n_log_h_). We now proceed with a more detailed description of the algorithm.

### Ternarization.

If the degree of a vertex of T is unbounded, then a partition into similarly sized connected subgraphs may not be possible. To fix this, we _ternarize_ T by replacing each vertex _v_ of degree _d(v_) larger than three by a path _P<sub>v</sub>_ of _d(v_)-2 vertices with degree three. Call the new vertices _virtual_ and let \(\mathcal{T}'\) denote the resulting tree. Each virtual vertex of _P<sub>v</sub>_ is incident in \(\mathcal{T}'\) to an (arbitrary) edge incident to _v_ in T except for the two endpoints of _P<sub>v</sub>_ that are incident to two such edges each. We maintain a link between each vertex in T and every associated virtual vertex in \(\mathcal{T}'\) (if any).

Let \(w'\) be a weight function on \(\mathcal{T}'\) obtained from _w_ by arbitrarily distributing weight from each deleted vertex to its associated virtual vertices. Note that T and _w_ can be obtained from \(\mathcal{T}'\) and \(w'\), respectively, by contracting every group of associated virtual vertices. Further bserve that \(|V(\mathcal{T}')|\le 2n\).

### Partition.

Fix a parameter _k_. We now compute a partition into \(\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{k})\) connected subgraphs of size at most 3_k_ as follows. Arbitrarily root \(\mathcal{T}'\). Iteratively remove minimal rooted subtrees of size at least _k_, using a simple linear-time bottom-up traversal. Since each node has at most three children, this produces connected subgraphs of size between _k_ and 3_k_. The only exception are the nodes remaining at the end, which we put into a possibly smaller subgraph. The total number of subgraphs is at most \(\frac{2n}{k}+1\).

### Building the super-tree.

By contracting each connected subgraph of the partition into a single vertex, we obtain a tree T, the _super-tree_, and a weight function _W_. We call each vertex \(A\in V(\mathfrak{T})\) a _super-vertex_, and write \(\mathcal{T}'[A]\) for the subgraph of \(\mathcal{T}'\) contracted into _A_. We write \(V(A)=V(\mathcal{T}'[A])\) for short. By definition of _W_ via the contraction, we have \(W(A)=w'(V(A))\).

Note that each _super-edge_ in _E_(T) is associated with precisely one normal edge in \(\mathcal{T}'\); we maintain an explicit link between the super-edge and the normal edge. For each super-vertex _A_, we build a top tree on<tbc>

\(\mathcal{T}'[A]\), and store the weight _W(A_). We call a vertex \(v\in V(A)\) that is adjacent to some vertex \(u\in\mathcal{T}'-V(A)\) a _boundary vertex_ of _A_, and maintain a list of boundary vertices for each super-vertex.

Constructing T and _W_ can be done in linear time. Setting up the top trees requires \(\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{k}\cdot k\mathrm{log}k)=\mathcal{O}(n\mathrm{log}k)\) time.

## Main procedure and recursion.

Below, we describe how to find a centroid and remove it, along with associated virtual vertices. Doing so may split up T (and implicitly T and \(\mathcal{T}'\)) into multiple connected components, on which we recurse. Hence, a recursive step operates on a tree T<sub>r</sub> (a subgraph of T ), a ternarization \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}\) of T<sub>r</sub>, and a super-tree T<sub>r</sub> on \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}\). Note that only T<sub>r</sub> is explicitly given, whereas T<sub>r</sub> and \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}\) are implicit in the super-tree data structure. Our task is to find a centroid _c_ of T<sub>r</sub> and remove it from T<sub>r</sub>, i.e., for each component H of T<sub>r</sub>-_c_, we return a super-tree on a ternarization of H.

## Finding centroids.

We now describe how to find a centroid of \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}\) using the super-tree T<sub>r</sub>. Note that, by Lemma 2.5, this is enough to find a centroid of T<sub>r</sub>.

First, we find the centroid _A_<sup>∗</sup> of T<sub>r</sub> with the trivial linear scan described in the introduction.

By Lemma 2.5, a centroid of \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}\) must be contained in \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}[A^*]\). We now construct a suitable weight function _w_<sup>∗</sup> on _V(A_<sup>∗</sup>) so that we can find a centroid of \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}\) within \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}[A^*]\). For each \(v\in V(A^*)\), let _C<sub>v</sub>_ be the connected component of \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}-(A^*-v)\) that contains _v_. Let \(w^*(v)=w'(C_v)\). Note that \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}[A^*]\) and _w_<sup>∗</sup> correspond to the tree and weight function obtained by contracting each _C<sub>v</sub>_ into a single vertex. If _C<sub>v</sub>_={_v_}, i.e., _v_ is not a boundary vertex, then there are no contractions and \(w^*(v)=w'(v)\).

We compute \(w'(C_v)\) for each boundary vertex _v_, and temporarily modify the weight of each _v_ in the top tree on _V(A_<sup>∗</sup>) to match _w_<sup>∗</sup>(_v_). Then, we find a centroid _c_ of \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}[A^*]\) w.r.t. _w_<sup>∗</sup>, and undo the weight change.<sup>5</sup>

By Lemma 2.5, a centroid of \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}\) must be contained in _C<sub>c</sub>_. We also know a centroid must be contained in _A_<sup>∗</sup>. Thus, by Lemma 2.2, a centroid must be contained in \(C_c\cap A^*=\{c\}\), so _c_ must be a centroid of \((\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r},w')\). If _c_ is not virtual, it also is a centroid of (T<sub>r</sub>_,w_). If it is virtual, the linked non-virtual vertex in T<sub>r</sub> is a centroid of (T<sub>r</sub>_,w_).

The running time to find _A_<sup>∗</sup> is O(|_V_(T<sub>r</sub>)|). Computing _w(C<sub>v</sub>_) for each boundary vertex _v_ can be done while traversing T<sub>r</sub>, also in O(|_V_(T<sub>r</sub>)|) time. There are at most \(\mathrm{deg}_{\mathfrak{T}_\mathrm{r}}(A^*)\le|V(\mathfrak{T}_\mathrm{r})|\) boundary vertices, so changing the weights in the top tree takes O(|_V_(T<sub>r</sub>)|log_k_) time.

## Splitting the data structure.

We now remove _c_ and its virtual vertices from \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}\) and T<sub>r</sub>. Let _R_ be the set of vertices to be removed. First, we remove each \(v\in R\) from its associated top tree by deleting all of its incident edges. This may split up each of the top trees into multiple new top trees. Each new top tree corresponds to a new super-vertex.

The creation of new super-vertices changes the super-tree, and may even split it up into a super-forest (see Figure 7 for an example). Let _A_ be a super-vertex from which we removed a vertex. For each boundary vertex _u_ of _A_, we find the new top tree that _u_ belongs to. Using this, we can compute all super-edges incident to the new super-vertices (recall that each super-edge corresponds to a normal edge between two boundary vertices in different super-vertices). Finally, we compute the connected components of the new super-forest F<sub>r</sub> using a simple traversal.

Removing a vertex _v_ from the top trees requires \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{deg}_{\mathcal{T}_\mathrm{r}^\prime}(v)\mathrm{log}k)\) time. Since each boundary vertex is the endpoint of an edge in T<sub>r</sub>, there are at most O(|_E_(T<sub>r</sub>)|) boundary vertices. The running time of recomputing the super-forest is thus O(|_E_(T<sub>r</sub>)|log_k_+|_V_(F<sub>r</sub>)|).

## Recursion.

After splitting, we recurse on each component of the super-forest that contains more than one (normal) vertex.

<sup>5</sup>Undoing the weight change is necessary, since we re-use the top tree data structures in later steps.

## Total running time.

The preprocessing time is O(_n_log_k_), as desired.

Consider one search-and-split step. Let \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}\) be the input tree, let T<sub>r</sub> be the input super-tree, let _R_ be the set of vertices removed in the splitting step, and let F<sub>r</sub> be the super-forest produced after splitting. The time required to execute the step is

\(\mathcal{O}\left((|V(\mathfrak{T}_\mathrm{r})|+|E(\mathfrak{T}_\mathrm{r})|)\mathrm{log}k+|V(\mathfrak{F}_\mathrm{r})|+\sum_{v\in R}\mathrm{deg}_{\mathcal{T}_\mathrm{r}^\prime}(v)\mathrm{log}k\right).\)

Since each vertex is removed only once, the third term sums up to O(_n_log_k_) over all vertices. The second term can be charged to recursive calls (for each component of F<sub>r</sub> with more than one normal vertex) or single vertices (for each component of F<sub>r</sub> consists of only one normal vertex). It remains to bound the first term.

If T<sub>r</sub> consists of only one super-vertex _A_, then we charge the O(log_k_) cost to the centroid of \(\mathcal{T}'_\mathrm{r}[A]\), for a total of O(_n_log_k_) over the course of the algorithm.

We analyze the other recursive calls in rounds. Assume that in each round, we execute one step on each remaining super-tree, thereby finding all centroids on a certain level of the centroid tree. Let F<sub>0</sub> be the initial super-tree, and let F_<sub>i</sub>_ be the forest of super-trees after round _i_. Note that the number of _edges_ cannot grow by splitting, so each F_<sub>i</sub>_ contains at most \(\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{k})\) edges, and therefore at most \(\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{k})\) non-isolated vertices, so the round requires \(\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{k}\mathrm{log}k)\) time in total.

If the height of the tree is _h_, then we have precisely _h_ rounds. Thus, the running time of the algorithm is \(\mathcal{O}((\frac{h}{k}+1)n\mathrm{log}k)\).

In particular, if we know _h_ and set _k=h_, then the running time is O(_n_log_h_). If we do not know _h_, we start with _k_=2 and run the algorithm for _k_ rounds. If it stops, then \(h\le k\) and we are done. Otherwise, try again with \(k\leftarrow k^2\). The last run of the algorithm, where \(h\le k\le h^2\), dominates the running time with O(_n_log_h_). Thus, we have

**Theorem 5.3.** _Let_ T _be a tree on n vertices and w be a positive weight function. We can compute a centroid tree of_ (T_,w_) _in time_ O(_n_log_h), where h is the height of the computed centroid tree._

## 5.2 Spread and zero-weight vertices

Let _w_ be a weight function on a tree T such that at least one vertex weight is positive. The _spread_ of _w_ is defined as \(\sigma_w=w(\mathcal{T})/min_{v\in V(\mathcal{T}),w(v)>0}w(v)\).

Let _T_ be a centroid tree of (T_,w_). By definition, if _u_ is a parent of _v_, then \(w(T_v)\le\frac{1}{2}w(T_u)\). More generally, if _v_ is at depth _d_, then \(w(T_v)\le 2^{-d}w(\mathcal{T})\). Thus, the depth of a positive-weight vertex _v_ cannot be more than \(1+log\frac{w(\mathcal{T})}{w(v)}\le 1+log\sigma_w\).

In particular, if all vertex weights are positive, then the height of every centroid tree is at most \(1+log\sigma_w\), so the algorithm of the previous section runs in time \(\mathcal{O}(nloglog\sigma)\).

If we allow zero-weight vertices, however, then this is not necessarily true, since there could be a large unbalanced zero-weight subtree. Also, the top-tree component of our algorithm does not allow zero weights for technical reasons. We believe that the top tree implementation of \[AHLT05\] can be adapted to this changed requirement, but for a simpler presentation, we prefer to use the standard interface, as defined in \[AHLT05\].

The solution to both problems is to change the zero weights by a very small amount, as follows. Let T be a tree on _n_ vertices, let \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), and let \(\varepsilon>0\). We define the positive weight function \(w_\varepsilon:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_+\) on _G_ as follows:

\(w_\varepsilon(v)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
w(v), & \text{if}w(v)\neq 0 \\
\varepsilon, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{array}\right.\)

We now prove that a centroid tree of \((\mathcal{T},w_\varepsilon)\) is also a centroid tree of (T_,w_) if \(\varepsilon\) is small enough. For this, it is enough to show that for every subgraph, no new centroids are introduced.

**Lemma 5.1.** _Let_ T _be a tree on n vertices, and let_ \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\)_. For each small enough_ \(\varepsilon>0\)_, each centroid of_ \((\mathcal{T},w_\varepsilon)\) _is a centroid of_ (T_,w)._

_Proof._ Let _k\<n_ be the number of zero-weight vertices w.r.t. _w_. Let _c_ be a centroid of (T_,g_) and let \(C\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-c)\). We have

\(w(C)\le w_\varepsilon(C)\le\frac{1}{2}w_\varepsilon(\mathcal{T})=\frac{1}{2}\left(w(\mathcal{T})+\varepsilon k\right)<\frac{1}{2}w(\mathcal{T})+\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon n.\)

If \(\varepsilon\) is small enough, this implies that \(w(C)\le\frac{1}{2}w(\mathcal{T})\). Repeating the argument for each \(C\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-c)\) shows that _c_ is a centroid of (T_,w_).

Note that if all weights are integers, we can simply set \(\varepsilon=1/n\) (or set \(\varepsilon=1\) and multiply each other weight by _n_). In general, we can treat \(\varepsilon\) symbolically, without explicitly computing a value for it.

We now show that the height of the centroid tree w.r.t. \(w_\varepsilon\) is essentially bounded by the spread of _w_; in other words, replacing _w_ with \(w_\varepsilon\) ensures that the computed centroid tree is "reasonable". Note that we can ignore the spread of \(w_\varepsilon\) here (which may be very large, if \(\varepsilon\) is very small).

**Lemma 5.2.** _Let_ T _be a tree on n vertices, let_ \(w:V(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\)_, and let_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _be defined as in Lemma 5.1. Each centroid tree of_ \((\mathcal{T},w_\varepsilon)\) _has height_ \(\mathcal{O}(log\sigma_w+logn)\).

_Proof._ Let _T_ be a centroid tree of \((\mathcal{T},w_\varepsilon)\). By Lemma 5.1, _T_ is also a centroid tree of (T_,w_). Thus, the depth of each node _v_ with _w(v)\>_0 is at most \(1+log\sigma_w\). Now consider a subtree _T<sub>u</sub>_ with _w(T<sub>u</sub>_)=0. Then the weight w.r.t. \(w_\varepsilon\) of each node in _T<sub>u</sub>_ is the same, so the spread of \(w_\varepsilon\) restricted to _V(T<sub>u</sub>_) is \(|V(T_u)|\le n\). This implies that the height of each zero-weight vertex in _T_ is at most \(2+log\sigma_w+logn\), concluding the proof.

Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 imply that we can replace _w_ with \(w_\varepsilon\) before running the algorithm. This yields

**Theorem 5.4** (Restatement of Thm. 1.5)**.** _Let_ T _be a tree on n vertices and w be a weight function. We can compute a centroid tree of_ (T_,w_) _in time_ \(\mathcal{O}(nlogh)\subseteq\mathcal{O}(nloglog\left(\sigma+n\right))\)_, where h is the height of the computed centroid tree and_ \(\sigma\) _is the spread of w._

### Handling many zero-weight vertices.

If almost all vertices have weight zero, then Theorem 5.4 can be improved (in terms of \(\sigma\)) by a preprocessing stage. We briefly sketch the argument.

Let T be the given tree, and _w_ be the given weight function. Let _m_ be the number of vertices with positive weight, and note that \(\sigma_w\ge m\). We first transform T by progressively removing zero-weight leaves, and replacing zero-weight degree-two vertices with an edge. This can be done with a single traversal in O(_n_) time. In the resulting tree \(\mathcal{T}'\), each zero-weight vertex has degree at least three (in particular, each leaf has positive weight). This means that at least half of the vertices in \(\mathcal{T}'\) have positive weight, so \(|V(\mathcal{T}')|\le 2m\). Computing a centroid tree _T_ on \(\mathcal{T}'\) thus requires \(\mathcal{O}(mloglog(\sigma_w+m))=\mathcal{O}(mloglog\sigma_w)\) time with Theorem 1.5 or O(_m_log_m_) with Theorem 5.3. The latter bound is better when \(\sigma_w\ge 2^m\).

It remains to show how to add the removed zero-weight vertices to the centroid tree _T_. Consider a maximal subgraph H of removed vertices. First compute a rooting _T_<sub>H</sub> of H; since all vertices in H have weight zero, _T_<sub>H</sub> is a centroid tree on H. Note that H has up to two neighbors in T , all with positive weight. Let _v_ be the neighbor of H that is farthest from the root in _T_, and attach _T_<sub>H</sub> to _T_ as a child of _v_. It is not hard to see that this requires O(_n_) time in total, and that the resulting search tree is a centroid tree of (T_,w_). Thus, we have

**Theorem 5.5.** _Let_ T _be a tree on n vertices and w be a weight function. We can compute a centroid tree of_ (T_,w_) _in time_ \(\mathcal{O}(n+mloglog\sigma)\) _or_ O(_n+m_log_m), where m is the number of vertices in_ T _with positive weight and_ \(\sigma\) _is the spread of w._

In particular, since \(m\le\sigma\), the running time becomes O(_n_) when \(\sigma\in\mathcal{O}(n/loglogn)\).

## 6.3 Optimal STTs

In this section we prove the characterization of optimal STTs as \(\alpha\)-centroid trees.

**Theorem 1.9.** _Let T be an optimal STT of_ (T_,w). Then, T is a_ \(\frac{2}{3}\)_-centroid tree of_ (T_,w)._

For the purpose of proving Theorem 1.9, we define the following transformation on search trees. Let _T_ be a search tree on T and \(v\in V(\mathcal{T})\). We denote by _T<sup>v</sup>_ the search tree on T that is obtained as follows. Set `root`(_T<sup>v</sup>_)=_v_. The subtrees of _T<sup>v</sup>_ rooted at the children of _v_ are all the trees of the form _T_|<sub>H</sub>, where \(\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-v)\). We say that _T<sup>v</sup>_ is obtained from _T_ by _lifting_ the vertex _v_. (This transformation can also be defined via _rotations_, e.g., see \[BCI<sup>+</sup>20\]. _T<sup>v</sup>_ is obtained by repeatedly rotating the edge between _v_ and its parent until _v_ becomes the root.) For every \(u,v\in V(\mathcal{T})\) we have

\(\mathtt{Path}_{T^v}(u)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\{v\}, & u=v \\
\{v\}\cup(\mathtt{Path}_T(u)\cap V(\mathcal{H})), & u\in V(\mathcal{H}),\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{T}-v).
\end{array}\right.\)

_Proof of Theorem 1.9._ Let _T_ be an optimal STT on T , and suppose towards contradiction, that _T_ is not a \(\frac{2}{3}\)-centroid. Assume w.l.o.g., that _w_(T)=1. By taking _T_ to be a minimum height counterexample, we can assume that the root _x_ of _T_ has a child _y_, so that \(w(T_y)>\frac{2}{3}\). Let _B<sub>x</sub>_ denote the set of vertices _not_ in the same component of T-_x_ as _y_, and let _B<sub>y</sub>_ denote the set of vertices not in the same component of T-_y_ as _x_. Finally, let _B<sub>x,y</sub>=V(T_)-_B<sub>x</sub>-B<sub>y</sub>_. By our assumption, \(w(B_y\cup B_{x,y})>\frac{2}{3}\), and thus, \(w(B_x)<\frac{1}{3}\). We distinguish three cases.

### Case 1.

If \(w(B_y)>\frac{1}{3}\), then transform _T_ by lifting _y_. The depths of vertices in _B<sub>y</sub>_ decrease by one and the depths of vertices in _B<sub>x</sub>_ increase by one. The depths of vertices in _B<sub>x,y</sub>_ are unchanged. (See Figure 10.1.) We have

\(\mathtt{cost}_w(T^y)-\mathtt{cost}_w(T)=w(B_x)-w(B_y)<\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=0,\)

contradicting the optimality of _T_.

If Case 1 did not occur, we have \(w(B_{x,y})>\frac{1}{3}\), and in particular, \(B_{x,y}\neq\emptyset\). Denote by _z_ the unique child of _y_ in _B<sub>x,y</sub>_.

### Case 2.

Assume _z_ is in the path in T between _x_ and _y_. Then, transform _T_ by lifting _z_. The depths of vertices in _B<sub>x</sub>_ increase by one, since each of these vertices gains _z_ as ancestor. The depths of vertices in _B<sub>y</sub>_ are unchanged, since these vertices gain _z_ and lose _x_ as ancestors. The depths of vertices in _B<sub>x,y</sub>_ are decreased by _at least_ one, since each loses at least one ancestor from {_x,y_}. (See Figure 10.2.) We then have

\(\mathtt{cost}_w(T^z)-\mathtt{cost}_w(T)\le w(B_x)-w(B_{x,y})<\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=0,\)

again, a contradiction.

### Case 3.

Finally, assume that _z_ is not in the path between _x_ and _y_. Note that this cannot happen in the special case of BSTs, i.e., when T is a path.

Let \(t\in B_{x,y}\) be the unique vertex in T whose removal separates _x_, _y_ and _z_ to different components. Now, transform _T_ by lifting _t_. As in the previous case, depths of vertices in _B<sub>x</sub>_ increase by one, depths of vertices in _B<sub>y</sub>_ stay the same and depths of vertices _B<sub>x,y</sub>_ decrease by _at least_ one. To see this, observe that each vertex in _B<sub>x,y</sub>_ gains _t_ as ancestor and loses two ancestors from {_x,y,z_}, and possibly more. (See Figure 10.3.) As in the previous case, we have `cost`_<sub>w</sub>(T<sup>t</sup>)\<_`cost`_<sub>w</sub>(T_), a contradiction.

## 7 Conclusions

We showed that the average search time in a centroid tree is larger by at most a factor of 2 than the smallest possible average search time in an STT and that this bound is tight. We also showed that centroid trees can be computed in O(_n_log_h_) time where _h_ is the height of the centroid tree.

Perhaps the most intriguing question is to determine whether the problem of computing an optimal STT is in P. A secondary goal would be to achieve an approximation ratio better than 2 in near linear time. (The running time of the STT’s of Berendsohn and Kozma \[BK22\] degrade as \(\mathcal{O}(n^{2k+1})\) for a \(\left(1+\frac{1}{k}\right)\)- approximation.) As for centroid trees, a remaining question is whether they can be computed in O(_n_) time whenever the spread of the weight function is \(\sigma\in\mathcal{O}(n)\).

A special case in which high quality approximation can be efficiently found is when an \(\alpha\)-centroid tree exists for \(\alpha<\frac{1}{2}\). This case can be recognized and handled in near linear time using our algorithm. (Observe that an \(\alpha\)-centroid tree for \(\alpha<\frac{1}{2}\) is also the unique \(\frac{1}{2}\)-centroid tree.) Theorem 1.7(ii) gives strong approximation guarantees for this case, yielding the _optimum_ when \(\alpha\le\frac{1}{3}\). It is an interesting question whether the bounds can be improved for \(\alpha\) in the range \(\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}\right)\), i.e., whether Theorem 1.7(ii) is tight.

A small gap remains in the exact approximation ratio of centroid trees when T has maximum degree \(\Delta\) and `OPT` is unbounded, i.e., between the upper bound \((2-\frac{1}{2^\Delta})\) of Theorem 1.3 and the lower bound \((2-\frac{4}{2^\Delta})\) of Theorem 1.4(ii).

**Theorem 2.1.** _Let T be a search tree on_ T _and_ H _a connected subgraph of_ T _. There is a unique search tree T_|<sub>H</sub> _on_ H _such that for every_ \(v\in V(\mathcal{H})\),<tbc>

\(\mathtt{Path}_{T|_\mathcal{H}}(v)=\mathtt{Path}_T(v)\cap V(\mathcal{H}).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ We denote by _u\<<sub>T</sub>v_ that _v_ is an ancestor of _u_ in _T_. We need to show that there is a unique search tree _T_|<sub>H</sub> on H such that for all \(u,v\in V(\mathcal{H})\),

\(u<_{T|_\mathcal{H}}v\Longleftrightarrow u<_Tv.\) (7)

_T_|<sub>H</sub> is constructed recursively as follows. Denote \(s=\mathtt{LCA}_T(\mathcal{H})\in V(\mathcal{H})\). Set _s_ as the root of _T_|<sub>H</sub>. The subtrees of _T_|<sub>H</sub> rooted at the children of _s_ will be all the trees _T|<sub>C</sub>_, where \(C\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{H}-s)\).

That _T_|<sub>H</sub> is a search tree on H is easily shown by induction on |_V_(H)|. Observing that (7) implies root(_T_|<sub>H</sub>)=`LCA`_<sub>T</sub>_(H), uniqueness also follows easily by induction. We show here by induction that (7) holds. Let \(u,v\in V(\mathcal{H})\) and let _r_=root(_T_|<sub>H</sub>). If _u_ and _v_ are in the same connected component \(C\in\mathbb{C}(\mathcal{H}-r)\), then by induction

\(u<_{T|_\mathcal{H}}v\Longleftrightarrow u<_{T|_C}v\Longleftrightarrow u<_Tv,\)

as required. If _u_ and _v_ are in two different connected components of H-_r_, then by construction, \(u\unknown\le_{T|_\mathcal{H}}v\). In that case since _r_=`LCA`_<sub>T</sub>_(H), we have _u\<<sub>T</sub>r_ and _v\<<sub>T</sub>r_, therefore also \(u\unknown\le_Tv\), as required. If _v=r_ then both _u\<<sub>T|<sub>H</sub></sub>v_ and _u\<<sub>T</sub>v_ hold. Finally, if _u=r_ then both \(u\unknown\le_{T|_\mathcal{H}}v\) and \(u\unknown\le_Tv\) hold.

We repeat here the definition of projection of a search tree given by Cardinal et al. \[CLP18\]. To avoid confusion, we denote by \(\tilde{T}|_\mathcal{H}\) the projection of _T_ to H as defined in \[CLP18\], and by _T_|<sub>H</sub> the projection as defined in Definition 2.1. We than show that in fact, \(\tilde{T}|_\mathcal{H}=T|_\mathcal{H}\).

As a preliminary step, Cardinal et al. show how to construct the projection of _T_ to T-_x_, where _x_ is a leaf of T . They distinguish between three cases:

1. _x_ has a parent and no child in _T_,<tbc>

2. _x_ has a parent and a single child in _T_,<tbc>

3. _x_=`root`(_T_).

In the first case, _x_ is simply removed from _T_. In the second case, _x_ is removed from _T_ and an edge is added between its parent and its child. In the third case, _x_ is removed and its only child is selected as the new root. This operation is referred to as _pruning x_ from _T_. The projection \(\tilde{T}|_\mathcal{H}\) is then defined as the tree obtained by iteratively pruning leaves that are not in H.

It is straightforward to verify that the pruning operation respects the equivalence (7). More precisely, if \(T'\) is obtained from _T_ by pruning _x_, then \(u\le_{T^\prime} v\Longleftrightarrow u\le_Tv\) whenever \(u,v\neq x\). By induction on the number of pruned vertices, it follows that

\(u\le_{\tilde{T}|_\mathcal{H}}v\Longleftrightarrow u\le_Tv\)

for all \(u,v\in V(\mathcal{H})\). That \(\tilde{T}|_\mathcal{H}=T|_\mathcal{H}\) follows from the uniqueness in Definition 2.1.
